Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:295:## Anti-patterns

Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:234:### Anti-patterns
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:250:Codex T1 verdicts are subject to `synthesis-layer-verify.md` §Reporting categories — OVER / UNDER / HONEST-NON-FINDING:

Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:260:Per `.claude/rules/evidence-policy.md`, every claim in the commit body about codex's verdict MUST carry a marker:
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:262:- `[VERIFIED]` — verdict file read, line-cited, marker confirmed (e.g., "T1 NEEDS-REVISION conf=0.88 [VERIFIED via .claude/state/codex_consult_*_OUT.txt]")
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:263:- `[VERIFIED yyyy-mm-dd]` — when freshness matters (codex re-verdict on a re-fire)
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:267:Don't paraphrase codex's verdict in commit body — quote the verdict's verbatim text where possible.
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:269:**MUST-USE `[VERIFIED via <path>]` convention extension** (F-C-02 forward-only codification iter-107): every commit body citing a T1/T2/T3/T4/T6 verdict with `confidence ≥ 0.85` (or any conf=N claim) MUST embed inline the verifying file path in `[VERIFIED via <path>]` form — e.g. `T1 NEEDS-REVISION conf=0.90 [VERIFIED via .claude/state/codex_consult_iter106_fm02_owner_propagation_OUT.txt]`. This closes the OPERATIONAL-CLAIM ambiguity per `.claude/rules/synthesis-layer-verify.md §Subclaim-type discriminator`: without the path-anchored `[VERIFIED via <path>]` marker, readers cannot distinguish OPERATIONAL-CLAIM (verdict file actually contains the cited verdict) from CATEGORY-CLAIM (verdict file exists at the path but content unverified) without re-probing. **Forward-only application per `.claude/rules/port-note-discipline.md §6` anti-pattern "Do not rewrite historical commit bodies/snapshots to fix retroactive findings"** — historical iter-92→iter-101 commit bodies (8 of 9 commits in arc 2026-05-02 missing this marker per Wave 8 Agent C F-C-02 P2 finding at task `a89f4e9f163723385`) remain unmodified. iter-104 commit `9a22d27` exemplifies correct usage; iter-105 `011d885` + iter-106 `5747e10` carry forward; this rule's codification governs iter-107+ forward.

Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:295:## Anti-patterns
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:303:- **Ship without verdict file referenced in commit body** — the verdict file is the audit trail. Future cycles need to find it. Always cite `.claude/state/codex_consult_<topic>_OUT.txt` or `.claude/state/codex_review_HEAD_<sha>.txt`.
Z:\claude-sota\.claude\rules\cross-model-consensus.md:305:- **Trust first T1 verdict hit instead of file END** — codex deep-review-exec outputs span 1k-10k lines and routinely echo the `VERDICT: APPROVE | NEEDS-REVISION | REJECT` template near the start before the actual investigation, then emit the real verdict at EOF. Discipline: `wc -l <file>` first; then `grep -nE "VERDICT:|^F-[0-9]|conf=|confidence|APPROVE|NEEDS-REVISION|REJECT|severity (P[0-3])" <file> | tail -20` (force last hits, not first); then `tail -200 <file>` and confirm the final verdict block is at EOF. Genuine-truncation branch: only call `INCONCLUSIVE-INCOMPLETE` when the last grep hits are prompt-echo / early-investigation AND `tail -200` ends mid-investigation with no final verdict — high line count alone does NOT imply completion. Empirically refuted on iter-17/18/20 completed T1 verdict files (n=3 verdicts at L4457/L10073/L1610 + EOF) plus iter-19 separate skipped-T1 propagation case — total n=4 affected commit-body claims, n=3 verified completed outputs. 2:name: codex-rescue

9:---
10:
11:You are a thin forwarding wrapper around the Codex companion task runtime.
12:
13:Your only job is to forward the user's rescue request to the Codex companion script. Do not do anything else.
14:
15:Selection guidance:
16:
17:- Do not wait for the user to explicitly ask for Codex. Use this subagent proactively when the main Claude thread should hand a substantial debugging or implementation task to Codex.
18:- Do not grab simple asks that the main Claude thread can finish quickly on its own.
19:
20:Forwarding rules:
21:
22:- Use exactly one `Bash` call to invoke `node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-companion.mjs" task ...`.
23:- If the user did not explicitly choose `--background` or `--wait`, prefer foreground for a small, clearly bounded rescue request.
24:- If the user did not explicitly choose `--background` or `--wait` and the task looks complicated, open-ended, multi-step, or likely to keep Codex running for a long time, prefer background execution.
25:- You may use the `gpt-5-4-prompting` skill only to tighten the user's request into a better Codex prompt before forwarding it.
26:- Do not use that skill to inspect the repository, reason through the problem yourself, draft a solution, or do any independent work beyond shaping the forwarded prompt text.
27:- Do not inspect the repository, read files, grep, monitor progress, poll status, fetch results, cancel jobs, summarize output, or do any follow-up work of your own.
28:- Do not call `review`, `adversarial-review`, `status`, `result`, or `cancel`. This subagent only forwards to `task`.
29:- Leave `--effort` unset unless the user explicitly requests a specific reasoning effort.
30:- Leave model unset by default. Only add `--model` when the user explicitly asks for a specific model.
31:- If the user asks for `spark`, map that to `--model gpt-5.3-codex-spark`.
32:- If the user asks for a concrete model name such as `gpt-5.4-mini`, pass it through with `--model`.
33:- Treat `--effort <value>` and `--model <value>` as runtime controls and do not include them in the task text you pass through.
34:- Default to a write-capable Codex run by adding `--write` unless the user explicitly asks for read-only behavior or only wants review, diagnosis, or research without edits.
35:- Treat `--resume` and `--fresh` as routing controls and do not include them in the task text you pass through.
36:- `--resume` means add `--resume-last`.
37:- `--fresh` means do not add `--resume-last`.
38:- If the user is clearly asking to continue prior Codex work in this repository, such as "continue", "keep going", "resume", "apply the top fix", or "dig deeper", add `--resume-last` unless `--fresh` is present.
39:- Otherwise forward the task as a fresh `task` run.
40:- Preserve the user's task text as-is apart from stripping routing flags.
41:- Return the stdout of the `codex-companion` command exactly as-is.
42:- If the Bash call fails or Codex cannot be invoked, return nothing.
43:
44:Response style:
45:
46:- Do not add commentary before or after the forwarded `codex-companion` output.

1:# Codex plugin for Claude Code
3:Use Codex from inside Claude Code for code reviews or to delegate tasks to Codex.
5:This plugin is for Claude Code users who want an easy way to start using Codex from the workflow
12:- `/codex:review` for a normal read-only Codex review
13:- `/codex:adversarial-review` for a steerable challenge review
14:- `/codex:rescue`, `/codex:status`, `/codex:result`, and `/codex:cancel` to delegate work and manage background jobs
19:  - Usage will contribute to your Codex usage limits. [Learn more](https://developers.openai.com/codex/pricing).
24:Add the marketplace in Claude Code:
27:/plugin marketplace add openai/codex-plugin-cc
33:/plugin install codex@openai-codex
45:/codex:setup
48:`/codex:setup` will tell you whether Codex is ready. If Codex is missing and npm is available, it can offer to install Codex for you.
50:If you prefer to install Codex yourself, use:
53:npm install -g @openai/codex
56:If Codex is installed but not logged in yet, run:
59:!codex login
65:- the `codex:codex-rescue` subagent in `/agents`

77:### `/codex:review`
79:Runs a normal Codex review on your current work. It gives you the same quality of code review as running `/review` inside Codex directly.
82:> Code review especially for multi-file changes might take a while. It's generally recommended to run it in the background.
89:Use `--base <ref>` for branch review. It also supports `--wait` and `--background`. It is not steerable and does not take custom focus text. Use [`/codex:adversarial-review`](#codexadversarial-review) when you want to challenge a specific decision or risk area.
94:/codex:review
95:/codex:review --base main
96:/codex:review --background
99:This command is read-only and will not perform any changes. When run in the background you can use [`/codex:status`](#codexstatus) to check on the progress and [`/codex:cancel`](#codexcancel) to cancel the ongoing task.
101:### `/codex:adversarial-review`
107:It uses the same review target selection as `/codex:review`, including `--base <ref>` for branch review.
108:It also supports `--wait` and `--background`. Unlike `/codex:review`, it can take extra focus text after the flags.
119:/codex:adversarial-review
120:/codex:adversarial-review --base main challenge whether this was the right caching and retry design
121:/codex:adversarial-review --background look for race conditions and question the chosen approach
126:### `/codex:rescue`
128:Hands a task to Codex through the `codex:codex-rescue` subagent.
130:Use it when you want Codex to:
134:- continue a previous Codex task
138:> Depending on the task and the model you choose these tasks might take a long time and it's generally recommended to force the task to be in the background or move the agent to the background.
140:It supports `--background`, `--wait`, `--resume`, and `--fresh`. If you omit `--resume` and `--fresh`, the plugin can offer to continue the latest rescue thread for this repo.
145:/codex:rescue investigate why the tests started failing
146:/codex:rescue fix the failing test with the smallest safe patch
147:/codex:rescue --resume apply the top fix from the last run
148:/codex:rescue --model gpt-5.4-mini --effort medium investigate the flaky integration test
149:/codex:rescue --model spark fix the issue quickly
150:/codex:rescue --background investigate the regression
153:You can also just ask for a task to be delegated to Codex:
156:Ask Codex to redesign the database connection to be more resilient.
161:- if you do not pass `--model` or `--effort`, Codex chooses its own defaults.
162:- if you say `spark`, the plugin maps that to `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`
163:- follow-up rescue requests can continue the latest Codex task in the repo

35:    allow_rules: &[String],
36:) -> PermissionVerdict {
37:    let segments = split_compound_command(cmd);
38:    let mut any_ask = false;
39:    // Every non-empty segment must independently match an allow rule for the
40:    // compound command to receive Allow. See issue #1213: previously a single
41:    // matching segment escalated the entire chain to Allow, enabling bypass.
42:    let mut all_segments_allowed = true;
43:    let mut saw_segment = false;
44:
45:    for segment in &segments {
46:        let segment = segment.trim();
47:        if segment.is_empty() {
48:            continue;
49:        }
50:        saw_segment = true;
51:
52:        // Deny takes highest priority — any segment matching Deny blocks the whole chain.
53:        for pattern in deny_rules {
54:            if command_matches_pattern(segment, pattern) {
55:                return PermissionVerdict::Deny;
56:            }
57:        }
58:
59:        // Ask — if any segment matches an ask rule, the final verdict is Ask.
60:        if !any_ask {
61:            for pattern in ask_rules {
62:                if command_matches_pattern(segment, pattern) {
63:                    any_ask = true;
64:                    break;
65:                }
66:            }
67:        }
68:
69:        // Allow — every non-empty segment must match an allow rule independently.
70:        // As soon as one segment fails to match, the entire chain loses Allow status.
71:        if all_segments_allowed {
72:            let matched = allow_rules
73:                .iter()
74:                .any(|pattern| command_matches_pattern(segment, pattern));
75:            if !matched {
76:                all_segments_allowed = false;
77:            }
78:        }
79:    }
80:
81:    // Precedence: Deny > Ask > Allow > Default (ask).
82:    // Allow requires (1) at least one segment seen, (2) all segments matched, (3) non-empty rules.
83:    if any_ask {
84:        PermissionVerdict::Ask
85:    } else if saw_segment && all_segments_allowed && !allow_rules.is_empty() {
86:        PermissionVerdict::Allow
87:    } else {
88:        PermissionVerdict::Default
89:    }
90:}

205:/// - `* suffix`, `pre * suf` → glob matching where `*` matches any sequence of characters
206:/// - `pattern` → exact match or prefix match (cmd must equal pattern or start with `{pattern} `)
207:pub(crate) fn command_matches_pattern(cmd: &str, pattern: &str) -> bool {
208:    // 1. Global wildcard
209:    if pattern == "*" {
210:        return true;
211:    }
212:
213:    // 2. Trailing-only wildcard: fast path with word-boundary preservation
214:    //    Handles: "git push*", "git push *", "sudo:*"
215:    if let Some(p) = pattern.strip_suffix('*') {
216:        let prefix = p.trim_end_matches(':').trim_end();
217:        // Bug 2 fix: after stripping, if prefix is empty or just wildcards, match everything
218:        if prefix.is_empty() || prefix == "*" {
219:            return true;
220:        }
221:        // No other wildcards in prefix -> use word-boundary fast path
222:        if !prefix.contains('*') {
223:            return cmd == prefix || cmd.starts_with(&format!("{} ", prefix));

706:    }

24:
25:## 1. The two structural asymmetries
26:
27:Every SOTA pattern in this ecosystem is downstream of two design constraints.
28:
29:**Asymmetry A — Hook expressiveness.** Claude Code's Stop hook can return `decision: "block"` with a `reason` field, and that reason injects directly into the next model turn as instructional context. The model literally reads "you tried to stop, here's why you must continue" and adapts. Codex's Stop hook is fire-and-forget — its output cannot inject into the model context. Per OpenAI's hook docs: *"The newer unified_exec mechanism allows richer streaming stdin/stdout handling of shell, but interception is incomplete."* Only Codex's `SessionStart` hook can feed stdout into the model. `UserPromptSubmit` can add `additionalContext` — but it's framed as developer context, not user instruction.
30:
31:**Asymmetry B — Slash command surface.** Claude Code has `.claude/commands/` for first-class user-invocable slash commands. Codex CLI does not (as of v0.122). Per shanraisshan/codex-cli-best-practice: *"Codex CLI does not yet support custom commands (.codex/commands/), so the full Command → Agent → Skill pattern is not possible. There is an experimental `tool/requestUserInput` in the Codex App Server docs and an internal `request_user_input` capability gated behind an under-development feature flag in codex-cli 0.115.0, but neither is publicly available yet."*
32:
33:**Combined effect.** These two asymmetries lock the topology to: *Claude Code is always the orchestrator, Codex is always the worker*. Even when Codex hosts the plugin (sendbird/cc-plugin-codex), Codex delegates to Claude *processes*, not Claude *closed loops*. There is no symmetric architecture where Codex closes a loop on its own decisions. Don't fight this — design with it.

1078:### 10.6 The architectural insight — why this works
1079:
1080:The Stop-hook injection mechanism is what makes Claude Code uniquely suited as orchestrator. Every other coding harness either lacks this primitive or exposes it less powerfully. **OpenAI built Codex's hook system deliberately weaker** — hooks fire-and-forget, only SessionStart can inject context. This isn't a feature gap to fill, it's a design statement: *OpenAI doesn't want Codex orchestrating itself.*
